title: When the Clock Turns
premise: In the waning months of a grinding border war, Astrid Lockridge completes the atlas her master died protecting, only to find a sealed letter hidden in its binding naming her family as complicit in a conspiracy to falsify the armistice boundary lines. When soldiers arrive to seize the atlas and silence the workshop, Astrid flees with the one unaltered master map and the letter, hunted by both the conspirators who want it destroyed and a disillusioned army cartographer who wants it used. Racing the armistice deadline, she must place the true map before the neutral commissioners before the victors' historians can burn the record — and decide whether justice means exposing her own family's name. She succeeds at terrible cost: the armistice is redrawn on honest lines, her family's innocence is proven, but the master's death is officially attributed to the enemy, and Astrid signs the atlas with a name that is no longer quite her own.
about_author: Coral Kavanagh is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing disputed border treaties and the people erased from them. She writes historical fiction about the clerks, mapmakers, and record-keepers who fight wars with ink instead of guns.

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. In the besieged port city of Verenholt, Astrid finishes inking the final plate of Master Edvard Lockridge's atlas while the war thuds distantly beyond the harbor. Edvard died three months ago under suspicious circumstances, and the guild pressures her to deliver the atlas to the Ministry. The beat is quiet grief and duty — the calm before the letter is found.

chapters.title: What the Binding Held
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Preparing the atlas for delivery, Astrid slits the spine's false backing and finds Edvard's sealed letter: proof that Ministry cartographers have been redrawing the boundary surveys, and a list of names — including her father's — marked as willing signatories. The emotional beat is betrayal and vertigo; the ground of her identity tilts.

chapters.title: The Orders Come
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, with a brief shift to her father Tomas. Ministry officers arrive to collect the atlas 'for the archives,' and Tomas hands it over with suspicious ease. Astrid, who secretly kept the master map and the letter, realizes her father may have signed something — or is protecting the family by cooperating. The beat is dread and fractured trust at the dinner table.

chapters.title: The Cartographer's Debt
chapters.summary: Captain Ilsa Reyne's POV. Ilsa, the army surveyor ordered to verify the falsified boundary, recognizes Edvard's survey marks on the 'official' maps and knows they're impossible. Ordered to burn the Lockridge workshop's remaining papers, she instead pockets one sheet. The beat is a soldier's crisis of conscience — power corrupting from the inside, witnessed.

chapters.title: Flight from Verenholt
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The workshop burns in the night — officially an enemy shell, unmistakably arson. Astrid flees with the master map sewn into her coat, leaving her brother to cover for her. The beat is terror and severance: the apprentice becomes a fugitive, measuring the world now in what can be carried.

chapters.title: The Neutral Ground
chapters.summary: Alternating Astrid and Ilsa. Both converge on the armistice commission at Lake Maren, where neutral commissioners will fix the border in eleven days. Ilsa catches Astrid forging commission credentials — then, instead of arresting her, proposes an uneasy alliance: her testimony plus Astrid's map against the Ministry's record. The beat is wary alliance between natural enemies.

chapters.title: The Historians' Fire
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. The conspirators move first: the Ministry's historians present a doctored survey archive, and the commissioners begin accepting it. Ilsa discovers her own name on the falsification roster — her career, her honor, conscripted. The beat is rage crystallizing into commitment; she is now inside the plot whether she likes it or not.

chapters.title: What the Name Is Worth
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid confronts her father, smuggled to the commission as a witness: he signed under coercion to protect the family after Edvard's murder, and his testimony could damn the conspirators — or hang him for treason. Astrid must choose between her family's safety and the truth on the record. The beat is the book's moral crux: identity versus justice.

chapters.title: The Eleventh Day
chapters.summary: Alternating Astrid and Ilsa. Climax. As the commissioners prepare to sign, the conspirators move to seize the master map; Ilsa holds the corridor with her rank and her confession, buying Astrid the minutes to unroll Edvard's true survey before the table, letter and map and her father's testimony laid down together. The beat is white-knuckle sacrifice — everything staked on ink and nerve.

chapters.title: A New Meridian
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, epilogue. The border is redrawn on honest lines; the conspirators fall, quietly, in the way power does. Edvard's death remains officially misattributed — the record corrected but the man unavenged — and Astrid signs the published atlas not as Lockridge's apprentice but under her own name, the first she has ever chosen. The beat is bittersweet resolution: justice outside the law, identity remade.
